X is not for nuance, so once you say something, you really can't take it back.
I don't think they understand how it's actually destroying their long term brand. Unfortunately, it hurts the people "under" them more than the person talking.
Case in point, I know of two folks who lost deals that were all set because of the drama going on X.
Given how much a commodity "capital" actually is and the sheer number of venture funds, you'd think people would be smarter than this.
But in this era of wanting airtime, I guess very few are playing long term games.

item.title: Cyber will be one of the most defining domains for AI in the coming years, and a huge area of focus for most enterprises. AI is going to now create a whole new level of work for security dealing with the increase of vibe coded issues, agentic attacks, and even accidental agent swarms hunting for da...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Cyber will be one of the most defining domains for AI in the coming years, and a huge area of focus for most enterprises.
AI is going to now create a whole new level of work for security dealing with the increase of vibe coded issues, agentic attacks, and even accidental agent swarms hunting for data. OpenAI + Hugging Face is just a preview of what’s to come.
Security teams have often been the most strapped for resources teams in the enterprise, and now it’s only going to get more intense. AI agents of course become the solution to this problem as well, and we’ll see a range of new agentic products for protecting code, enterprise systems, mission critical infrastructure, and enterprise data. Huge opportunity here right now.
And it’s going to be a booming market for cyber professionals that can effectively deploy agents for security purposes in the enterprise. Great time to be in security.

item.title: I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude. Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out. Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, y...
item.description:
作者：Boris Cherny 账号：@bcherny 简介：Claude Code @anthropicai
I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude.
Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out.
Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model:
1. What you want it to do 2. How much effort you want it to spend 3. How it should verify that it did the right thing

item.title: Ep 94: Applied Compute CEO on the Limits of RL, the New AI Hyperscaler & Why Post-Training Wins Inference
item.description:
播客：Unsupervised Learning
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:02 How do you kind of characterize where we are today?
Speaker 2 | 00:02 - 00:25 What we have with RL is we essentially have a hill climbing machine. The hardest part is actually defining the hill to climb, which is why evals, I think, is like a really important thing for companies to, a, focus on building and b, actually like safeguard pretty carefully. Your employees are not fungible. You would not like be comfortable with them going to another company and doing work there. And same thing with these models.
Speaker 1 | 00:29 - 01:07 Owning your own intelligence and training your own models is incredibly in the AI zeitgeist these days. There's probably no better person to speak with about all these topics than Josh from Applied Compute. Applied Compute is working with a bunch of the most cutting edge AI applications on a really interesting post training examples. Josh and I were able to talk about his perspective on a bunch of the top questions around open models today, including when it actually makes sense to post train these models, how to think about the future of when this stuff makes sense, especially as the labs, you know, get more and more data from different domains over time. We also talked about, like, when it makes sense to harness optimize versus actually go and post train, as well as just get Yash's thoughts on a lot of the really interesting things happening in the ecosystem today.
Speaker 1 | 01:07 - 01:18 All in all, it's a fascinating conversation with a brilliant mind in the space. I hope folks enjoyed as much as I did. Without further ado, here's Yacht. Well, thanks so much for for coming on the podcast.
Speaker 2 | 01:18 - 01:19 Thank you for having me.
Speaker 1 | 01:19 - 01:22 Yeah. Been looking forward to this one for for a while.
Speaker 2 | 01:22 - 01:27 Yeah. Yeah. No. It's it's been a long time coming. It's good we can finally do it in person as well.
Speaker 1 | 01:27 - 01:30 Yes. Always better in person in our little like closet of a studio here.
Speaker 2 | 01:30 - 01:36 Yeah. This is this is awesome. I mean, like, it's very cozy, built built exactly for the setting.
Speaker 1 | 01:36 - 01:39 Yeah. Definitely not a repurposed library. Yeah. Or like, purpose built
Speaker 2 | 01:39 - 01:42 for Yeah. For podcasts. So thanks for having me.
Speaker 1 | 01:42 - 01:44 Of course. Well, I feel like there's a bunch
Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:45 of places we could start, but
Speaker 1 | 01:45 - 02:14 where thought would be most interesting for our listeners is just owning your own intelligence feels like it's in the zeitgeist. I don't know, you know, when the tipping point happened, you know, three or four months ago, but like, it is certainly, you know, the conversation. And I feel like there's been a bunch of different versions articulated of the risk There's of depending on Frontier been people saying, you know, you'll never know when they'll pull the APIs away, when they decide, you know, something's a safety risk and they don't give you access. There's been, you know, they'll build products and compete with you. They'll be, if you use their models, they'll train on your data.
Speaker 1 | 02:14 - 02:24 Yeah. There's all sorts of different arguments. And I'm curious, you think about like this, you know, the case for this, which of these arguments like resonate for you? Which of them do you think maybe are a little overblown? Yeah.
Speaker 2 | 02:25 - 02:30 Yeah. So so, you know, I... As as as you know, my background is I actually worked at a Yeah.
Speaker 1 | 02:30 - 02:32 You've seen in the inside. Labs.
Speaker 2 | 02:32 - 03:05 And I think, like, the the risks or not even risks, just the things that I think about when it comes to owning your intelligence aren't more the ones that are like, presumed that the labs are malicious or something like that, where they're stealing your data or whatnot. I think like, you know, these companies are made up of great people. There are contractual obligations. There's actual you know, there's a lot of engineering that goes in protecting data and whatnot. But I do think that the idea of owning your intelligence really is about flexibility and control.
Speaker 2 | 03:05 - 03:39 And so you said like, oh, I don't know when this own your intelligence narrative popped up. I think it really popped up when the open model started getting good and you could actually go and do things with them. But the control you get, it can actually be a lot deeper than that, right? Like where these models run, how you deploy them, what you optimize them, whether it's cost or latency or specific domains, the more control you get, that's what we're talking about when when we say own your intelligence. So if you wanna own your intelligence and you wanna be able to train these models to do tasks on your data, you actually need to have access to the weights.
Speaker 2 | 03:39 - 04:02 You need to have the infrastructure to post train them, to inference them, to route between them. You know, I do think there are risks about being super dependent on a single model vendor. Luckily, think, like, the the the labs are doing their best to sort of, like, serve as many people as possible. But there are times when models can get pulled from different products. That's happened actually more than once, particularly in the coding space.
Speaker 2 | 04:02 - 04:34 And so, you know, I think as these labs start to move more into specific verticals, like, you know, it's not clear whether they won't... They'll continue serving companies that are... They're directly competing against. And so the safest sort of like most durable thing that you can go and do and the advantage you can build up, think, is investing in the full stack to be able to make models that are powering your products, that are intelligent, that are doing the things that you want, and not having, like, extreme vendor dependence on any one set of models
Speaker 1 | 04:34 - 04:49 or companies. And it feels like this this narrative has really won out. Mean, I think maybe one of the most interesting manifestations of is even yesterday, OpenAI announcing like this partnership with Base10, right, where you can kind of use OpenAI credits almost burn them down on on on open models through Base10.
Speaker 2 | 04:49 - 05:07 So I I think first of all, we're we're big admirers of the Base10 team. And and I think that Tuan and Danny and all of those folks, they're really an incredible company. But yeah, I think I think this was a clear signal that like, hey, this is multi model future. Customers want choice. They want flexibility.
Speaker 2 | 05:07 - 05:25 I think on the OpenAI side, it's a clear sort of motion towards, hey, we wanna be more of a platform. I don't know if you noticed this, but the narrative a couple months ago was definitely like, hey, like we are going to talk about and sort of promote and analyze the strongest, biggest, baddest model out there. And now it's like much more talking about a Pareto curve.
